itemList.description: Removing water hyacinth from the Khandige River Belt through mechanical intervention is a vital ecological measure to restore river health and protect aquatic life. The operation will be carried out under the supervision of the Engineer-in-charge using a coordinated approach that combines manual labour, appropriate materials, machinery, and motor boats equipped with perforated excavator buckets to efficiently extract the invasive weed. This comprehensive effort, executed at approved rates, covers all associated costs including labour, transportation of men and materials, motor boat rental, excavator and tipper hire. By controlling the rapid proliferation of water hyacinth-which depletes oxygen and blocks sunlight essential for fish and other organisms-he project ensures ecological balance, safeguards biodiversity, and promotes the long-term sustainability of the river ecosystem.

Safe disposal of water hyacinth removed from the Khandige River Belt with required efficiency, ecological responsibility, and worker safety. The process involves the use of excavators, tippers, and other related machinery to collect, transport, and dispose of the weed in designated areas approved by the supervising authority. Excavators fitted with perforated buckets will lift and load the hyacinth onto tippers, which will then transport the material to disposal sites, ensuring no spillage along transit routes. All machinery must be operated by trained personnel under the supervision of the Engineer-in-charge, with strict adherence to safety protocols such as proper signaling, use of protective gear, and controlled movement of equipment near water bodies. The specification also covers associated costs including labour, machinery hire, fuel, and transportation, ensuring that the operation is executed at approved rates. By following this coordinated approach, the project guarantees safe disposal of the invasive weed, prevents its re-entry into the river system, and supports the long-term restoration of ecological balance and biodiversity.
